why_how.text: Pedestrians face the greatest danger of all road users.
Drivers must yield to walkers in every crosswalk and watch for children and travelers with disabilities.

scenario.text: Lee is turning left at a corner as a man with a white cane steps into the crosswalk against the signal.

reasoning.text: Blind travelers with dogs or white or metal canes command absolute crossing priority over signals.

result.text: Lee stops and waits for the man to finish crossing.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking an unmarked crosswalk gives pedestrians less priority than a painted one.

correction.text: Marked and unmarked crosswalks grant walkers equal priority, with every approach yielding.

memory_support.text: Every crosswalk is theirs; a cane or dog crosses first.

prompt.text: Another car has stopped to let a pedestrian cross. May you pass it?

answer.text: No, never pass a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian.

rationale.text: Stopped-for-walker vehicles, like red-lit school buses, freeze all passing.

narration.text: This chapter covers sharing the road with everyone else who uses it: large vehicles, bicycles, motorcycles, mopeds, walkers, skaters, scooters, slow-moving vehicles and horses. Each has its own quirks and duties. We begin with pedestrians, who face the greatest danger. The manual points to places that draw children, such as schools, bus stops, playgrounds, parks and ice-cream trucks, and to everyday risks like backing out of a driveway. In this lesson we cover how walkers should behave, how drivers should turn, back and stop around them, and when you must never pass another vehicle.

lines.text: Turning: watch walkers on the near and far side.
Cane or guide dog: absolute priority.

narration.text: Where there is no sidewalk, walkers should keep to the side of the road facing traffic. When you turn right, watch for walkers on your right; when you turn left, watch for walkers on the far side. A blind traveler with a guide dog or a white or metal cane has absolute priority when crossing, over any signal. Keep your eyes sweeping the edges of the road. Walkers have duties too: they must obey signals, use the sidewalk or walk facing traffic, and not sell things at the roadside. So both sides share responsibility, but the driver must always yield to a blind traveler.

lines.text: Look twice; no phones or headphones.

narration.text: The manual's tips for drivers start with staying alert, being seen, and scanning. Assume that pedestrians may break rules anywhere, at any time. Look twice in all directions, and be especially careful when turning left, which the manual singles out as a major source of pedestrian injuries in the city. Never drive impaired or tired, and put away phones, texting, other devices and headphones. These habits matter most where walkers are common, but the manual's point is that a pedestrian can appear anywhere, so the habits should be with you on every drive, not only in busy places.

lines.text: Check for small children before backing.
Hang back at stops for a clear view.

narration.text: Before backing, check again for small children behind you, through clean, well-lit windows. Walkers have the right-of-way in every crosswalk, marked or not, and even where there is no signal, you yield to anyone in danger. Every approach to a crosswalk yields. Crashes, injuries and failing to take due care can all bring tickets. When you stop, hang back far enough to keep a clear view, and yield to walkers on every turn. So the crosswalk, painted or not, is the walker's space, and your job is to stop early enough that both of you can see each other.

lines.text: Never pass a car stopped for a walker.

narration.text: Expect travelers with disabilities and respect guide dogs, canes and other devices. Take special care with children and older people. Never block or park on a crosswalk. Stop for a school bus with red lights flashing. Never pass a vehicle that has stopped for a pedestrian. Obey speed limits and stop signs, take extra care in low visibility, slow before crosswalks, back carefully, watch for blind spots behind roof pillars, never pass at crossings, and creep through school zones, blocks with children and intersections. All of these rules point the same way: when walkers may be present, slow down and yield.

lines.text: Stopped buses and cars: no passing.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers think a crosswalk without paint does not count, or that they may pass a car that has stopped for no obvious reason. The manual says marked and unmarked crosswalks grant walkers equal priority, with every approach yielding, and red-lit school buses plus vehicles stopped for walkers freeze all passing. So treat every corner as a crosswalk, whether it is painted or not. And if the car beside or ahead of you has stopped at a crossing, assume someone is walking in front of it, and stop too, rather than going around it.

lines.text: A car stopped for a walker.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: the car in the next lane has stopped to let a pedestrian cross. May you pass it? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Never pass a vehicle that has stopped for a pedestrian. Like a school bus with red lights flashing, a vehicle stopped for a walker freezes all passing. Remember too that marked and unmarked crosswalks give walkers equal priority, and that a blind traveler with a guide dog or a white or metal cane always has absolute priority, whatever the signal shows. Stop for the stopped car, every time.

lines.text: Never pass a car stopped for a walker.

narration.text: To close, many kinds of road users share the road, and pedestrians face the greatest danger, so take extra care near schools, bus stops, playgrounds, parks and ice-cream trucks, and look through the rear window when backing. Walkers face traffic where there is no sidewalk, turning drivers watch walkers on both sides, and a blind traveler with a dog or a white or metal cane always crosses first. Look twice, expect rule-breaking and put devices away. Walkers own every crosswalk, marked or not. Stop for red-lit school buses, and never pass a vehicle stopped for a walker. Next come bicyclists.

why_how.text: Cyclists travel the same way as cars but are fragile, so drivers must give them room.
Cyclists have their own rules on lane position, equipment and passengers.

scenario.text: Dana is about to open her car door on a street where cyclists ride by.

reasoning.text: Drivers head-check blind spots before turns, parking, opening doors and pulling from the curb.

result.text: Dana checks over her shoulder, waits for a cyclist to pass, then opens the door.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking cyclists must always stay at the far right edge.

correction.text: Riders hold lanes or right edges except when turning left or dodging hazards.

memory_support.text: Two abreast at most, helmets through thirteen, lights at five, three and two hundred feet.

prompt.text: At night, from how far must a bicycle's rear lamp be visible?

rationale.text: The front lamp shows five hundred feet ahead and a side lamp two hundred feet.

narration.text: This lesson covers sharing the road with bicyclists. Cyclists travel in the same direction as other traffic, but they are much more exposed, so drivers need to check blind spots and give them room. The manual also sets out the rules cyclists must follow: where they ride, how many may ride side by side, who must wear a helmet, how they signal, who may ride as a passenger, and what equipment and lights a bicycle needs. Finally, it explains how drivers should turn and pass near cyclists. Knowing the cyclist's rules helps you predict what a rider will do next.

Cyclists share the road traveling the same way as cars, but they are fragile and can be hard to see. So before you turn, park, open a door or pull away from the curb, check your blind spots over your shoulder. Give cyclists room, and when you pass, slow down so the air you push does not unsettle them. Be ready for sudden moves, much as you would with a motorcycle, because a cyclist may swerve to avoid a hazard you cannot see. Treat a cyclist as a road user who needs extra space, not as an obstacle to squeeze past. Room, slow passes and head checks are the driver's part.

lines.text: In the lane or at the right edge.
Helmets for ages one to thirteen.

narration.text: Cyclists ride in the lane or at the right edge, without blocking traffic, except when they are about to turn left or must avoid a hazard. They must stop fully before entering the road from a driveway, alley or curb. They may ride at most two abreast, and they must stay off sidewalks where riding is banned. Riders aged one to thirteen must wear approved helmets, and adults follow local rules. The manual sums up the position rule: riders hold the lane or the right edge except when turning left or dodging hazards, pair at most two abreast, and wear a helmet through age thirteen.

lines.text: Brakes and a bell heard at one hundred feet.
Night: front, rear and side lamps.
Reflectors on spokes, rear and pedals.

narration.text: A bicycle on the highway needs brakes and a bell that can be heard one hundred feet away. At night it also needs a front lamp visible five hundred feet ahead, a rear lamp visible three hundred feet behind, and at least one lamp visible two hundred feet to each side, along with spoke, rear and pedal reflectors. Cyclists and motorists share the same rights and duties toward each other. So drivers yield to cyclists, respect their speed, scan for them in parking lots, watch for them when backing, parking or opening doors, and learn the hand signals cyclists use.

Here is the trap. The three bicycle light distances are easy to mix up. The manual lays them out as a three-rung visibility ladder: night cycles show front lamps five hundred feet ahead, rear lamps three hundred feet behind, and one lamp two hundred feet to each side. So the numbers fall as you go from front to rear to side. Do not confuse them with the bell, which must be heard one hundred feet away. For a driver, the point is that a properly equipped bicycle should be visible from a good distance at night, so watch for those lights.

lines.text: Right on red: scan right and behind.
Pass slowly, with a lane change.
Bike lanes and boxes are not for cars.

narration.text: Before turning right on red, scan to the right and behind for cyclists, stop fully, and look left, right, left and behind again. When passing a cyclist, limit the pass, drive defensively, change lanes if you can, watch for opening doors, slow down, and be ready for the rider to swerve. Bike lanes, bike boxes, two-way bike tracks and green-painted areas are all off limits to drivers. And although cyclists must follow the same road rules, drivers should still expect some cyclists to break them, and drive with that possibility in mind.

lines.text: How far must the rear lamp show?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: at night, from how far must a bicycle's rear lamp be visible? Work it out before reading on. The answer is three hundred feet. The front lamp must be visible five hundred feet ahead, and at least one lamp must show two hundred feet to each side. The bell must be heard one hundred feet away. Remember the cyclist's position rule too: riders keep to the lane or the right edge except when turning left or avoiding hazards, ride at most two abreast, and wear helmets through age thirteen. Look right and behind before every right turn near cyclists.

lines.text: Lights at five, three and two hundred feet.

narration.text: To wrap up, cyclists travel the same way as cars but are fragile, so head-check before turning, parking, opening doors or leaving the curb, and pass slowly with room. Cyclists ride in the lane or at the right edge except to turn left or avoid hazards, at most two abreast, and riders aged one to thirteen wear helmets. They use hand signals, carry children under one never and children one to four only in attached seats, and report serious crashes within ten days. Bicycles need brakes, a bell heard at one hundred feet, and night lamps visible five hundred feet ahead, three hundred behind and two hundred to the side.

why_how.text: Skaters, scooter riders and motorcyclists are as exposed as cyclists and deserve due care.
Motorcycles are hard to see and judge, so drivers must actively look for them.

scenario.text: Kai is about to turn left and sees what looks like a distant motorcycle approaching.

reasoning.text: Small profiles fake distance and speed, and left-turning vehicles meet many fatal riders.

result.text: Kai waits for the motorcycle to pass before turning.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a car may share a lane with a motorcycle because the bike is narrow.

correction.text: Two motorcyclists may share a lane, yet no rider may share or pass within a lane holding any non-motorcycle vehicle.

memory_support.text: Look for the bike before you turn left.

prompt.text: A friend says it is fine to ride beside a motorcycle in the same lane if it is narrow. Is that right?

rationale.text: Two motorcyclists may ride side by side in one lane, but no rider may share a lane with a car.

title.text: Riders who are easy to miss

lines.text: Why motorcycles are hard to see.

narration.text: This lesson covers skaters, skateboarders, scooter riders and motorcyclists. Like cyclists, they are exposed and vulnerable, and drivers owe them due care. Motorcycles get special attention in the manual, because they are common in New York and because drivers so often fail to see them. We will cover why motorcycle crashes are so harmful to riders, why a motorcycle's speed and distance are hard to judge, how motorcycles use the lane, why their lights and signals can mislead, where crashes tend to happen, and the road hazards that make riders swerve. The aim is to train your eyes to find riders.

lines.text: Small profile fakes distance and speed.

narration.text: A motorcycle's small profile, seen from any angle, makes it hard to judge how far away it is and how fast it is going. Riders move around within their lane, and two may legally ride side by side, though they may never share a lane with, or pass within the lane of, a car or other vehicle. Larger vehicles can hide a motorcycle during passing and merging. So when you look for traffic, a motorcycle may be closer and faster than it seems, or hidden behind a truck. Give it more time and space than your first impression suggests, especially before you pull out or turn.

Motorcycle lights can make them harder, not easier, to notice. Their always-on headlights blend in among cars with daytime running lights. Their small tail lights are always on, which makes braking harder to see, and they lack a brake light at eye level. Their turn signals sit close to the headlight and may not cancel by themselves, which can confuse other drivers. And at intersections, drivers tend to look for larger vehicles first, which lets motorcycles blend in, sometimes fatally. So do not rely on a motorcycle's lights or signals to tell you what it is doing.

lines.text: Two motorcycles may share a lane.
A car may not share a motorcycle's lane.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because a motorcycle is narrow, some drivers think they can share its lane or squeeze past it within the lane. The manual says two motorcyclists may share one lane side by side, yet no rider may share or pass within a lane holding any non-motorcycle vehicle. So a motorcycle gets a full lane, just like a car. When you pass one, change lanes completely. And when two riders share a lane, that is legal for them, but it does not open space for you in that lane. Treat every motorcycle as a full vehicle for lane purposes.

The manual cites crash data showing that drivers turning left are involved in a large share of fatal motorcycle crashes, against riders going straight, passing or overtaking. Many motorcycle crashes involve more than one vehicle. The lesson the manual draws is that drivers must retrain their eyes, which tend to look only for cars, into scans that look for many hazards at once: trucks, buses, bicycles, pedestrians and motorcycles. So before you turn left in particular, look deliberately for a motorcycle coming toward you, rather than only checking for cars.

lines.text: Riders swerve around gravel and debris.
Do not tailgate; leave room in rain.

narration.text: Road surface problems that a car barely notices can be dangerous for a rider. Motorcyclists swerve around gravel, debris, pavement seams, manhole covers and animals. At railroad crossings they slow down, rise up and cross the rails squarely. On steel bridge decks they ride in the center of the lane and need generous following gaps. So never tailgate a motorcycle, because a rider can stop in a shorter distance than you expect and the reason may be hidden from you. Leave even more space in rain and in the dark, and pass a rider gently, without a blast of air.

Here is a quick check: may a car share a lane with a motorcycle? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Two motorcyclists may share one lane side by side, but no rider may share or pass within a lane that holds any non-motorcycle vehicle. So when you pass a motorcycle, change lanes completely. Remember why motorcycles are so easy to miss: their small profile fakes distance and speed, their lights blend in, and their signals may not cancel. And before you turn left, look deliberately for an oncoming rider.

lines.text: Due care for skaters and scooters.

narration.text: To close, skaters, skateboarders and scooter riders share the cyclist's vulnerability and deserve due care, and motorcyclists have the same rights and duties as every driver. Motorcycles can appear at any time, and riders suffer far worse injuries because no frame protects them. A motorcycle's small profile fakes distance and speed, two may share a lane but never with a car, and its lights and signals can mislead. Drivers turning left are a major danger to riders, so retrain your eyes to look for motorcycles among every other hazard. Give riders room around gravel, rails and steel decks, and never tailgate them.

why_how.text: Moped classes depend on top speed and set different license and lane rules.
Large trucks have deep blind spots that hide cars.

scenario.text: Nina buys a moped whose top speed is twenty-five miles per hour.

reasoning.text: Class B mopeds run twenty-one to thirty and take any-class licenses with right-lane limits.

result.text: Nina rides at the right edge with plates, lights, helmet and eye gear, and insurance.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any moped may use an expressway.

correction.text: Every moped shuns expressways unless signs invite, and Classes B and C hug the right edge.

memory_support.text: A fast, B middle, C slow; B and C keep right.

prompt.text: Your neighbor buys a moped that reaches thirty-five miles per hour. What license must she hold to ride it?

rationale.text: Class A runs thirty-one to forty, while Classes B and C take any class of license.

narration.text: This lesson covers two very different kinds of vehicle. First, mopeds, which come in three classes based on top speed. Each class has its own license, lane, equipment and insurance rules, so it helps to keep them straight. Second, large trucks, which the manual describes as having blind spots so deep that they form no-zones around the vehicle. We will sort the moped classes, look at where mopeds may ride, and then begin on large trucks, which the next lesson continues. Both topics come down to knowing what the other vehicle can and cannot do.

lines.text: Class A: thirty-one to forty, motorcycle license.

narration.text: Mopeds are classed by top speed. Class A reaches thirty-one to forty miles per hour and needs a motorcycle license; it may use any lane and needs plates, lights, a helmet and eye protection, and insurance. Class B reaches twenty-one to thirty, and Class C twenty or less; both may be driven with any class of license, are limited to the right lane, and need plates and lights. Class B also needs a helmet, eye gear and insurance, while for Class C those are recommended, except where rentals require them. Safety responsibility rules apply to all classes, and junior and permit rules still apply.

lines.text: Classes B and C: right edge.

narration.text: Class B and C mopeds keep to the right edge of the road, while Class A may use any lane. No moped may use an expressway unless signs allow it. Mopeds also make left turns only from the proper lanes, and riders need reflective clothing and certified eye protection. Inspection and title duties vary by class. Drivers should approach mopeds with the same care they give cyclists. So the moped's class tells you where to expect it: at the right edge for Classes B and C, possibly anywhere in the lane for Class A, and on an expressway only where a sign permits.

lines.text: Class A: motorcycle license, any lane.
Classes B and C: any license, right lane.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People treat all mopeds alike. The manual sorts them: Class A mopeds reach thirty-one to forty with motorcycle licenses and any-lane rights, while B reaches twenty-one to thirty and C twenty or less, with any-class licenses and right-lane limits. And lower mopeds hug right edges, Class A roams freely, and every moped shuns expressways unless signs invite. So the top speed sets the class, and the class sets the license and the lane. A rider on a fast Class A moped needs a motorcycle license, while a Class C rider needs only an ordinary license and keeps right.

lines.text: Car drivers blamed in most car-truck fatal crashes.
A front blind zone ahead of long hoods.

narration.text: The manual cites data showing that in fatal crashes between cars and trucks, car drivers are most often to blame, and most of the people killed are in the car. Large trucks need more room to stop and pass, and they have large blind spots. There are deep shadows along the sides and behind the truck, and on trucks with long hoods, a blind zone that reaches about twenty feet in front. These are called no-zones. So the size of a truck works against the car driver: it hides you from the truck driver and gives the truck less room to avoid you.

Here is a quick check: what license does a Class A moped require? Work it out before reading on. The answer is a motorcycle license. Class A mopeds reach thirty-one to forty miles per hour and may use any lane, while Class B, at twenty-one to thirty, and Class C, at twenty or less, may be driven with any class of license and must keep to the right lane. No moped may use an expressway unless signs allow it. And when you drive near a moped of any class, give it the same care you would give a cyclist. Speed sets the class, and the class sets the license and the lane.

lines.text: A fast, B middle, C slow.

narration.text: To wrap up, mopeds are classed by top speed. Class A reaches thirty-one to forty miles per hour, needs a motorcycle license and may use any lane. Class B reaches twenty-one to thirty and Class C twenty or less; both may be driven with any license and keep to the right lane. Class A and B need helmets, eye gear and insurance, while for Class C they are recommended. No moped uses an expressway unless signs allow, and drivers treat mopeds with cyclist-grade care. Large trucks have deep blind spots along the sides and rear and a front blind zone on long-hood trucks. Next we continue with trucks.

why_how.text: Trucks hide cars in their blind spots, stop slowly and turn wide.
Slow-moving vehicles, all-terrain vehicles, snowmobiles and horses need careful handling.

scenario.text: Sam passes a large truck on the highway and wants to return to its lane.

reasoning.text: Returns wait for the truck's full front in the mirror, and cutoffs stay banned.

result.text: Sam waits until he can see the whole front of the truck in his mirror, then moves back.

claim.text: Common mistake: slipping behind a truck that is backing up.

correction.text: Backing rigs command waiting rather than slipping through their blind spots.

memory_support.text: See the full front before you return; wait for backing trucks.

prompt.text: You come up behind a farm tractor showing a reflective orange triangle. What is the triangle telling you?

answer.text: The vehicle is slow-moving, so pass with caution.

rationale.text: The triangle flags animal-drawn, farm, construction and rural-mail vehicles.

narration.text: This last lesson of the chapter continues with large trucks and then turns to vehicles and animals that move slowly. The manual explains where trucks hide cars, why they need more room to stop, how they turn, and how to pass them, wait for them, and stop behind them. Then it covers slow-moving vehicles marked with orange triangles, all-terrain vehicles and snowmobiles crossing the road, and horses and their riders. The chapter closes with review questions. Much of this lesson is about patience: giving large and slow vehicles the room and time they need.

lines.text: Do not linger beside a truck.
Never cut off; expect a left swing.

narration.text: Cars that linger beside a truck disappear into its side blind spots, and stickers on the back of a truck can block the view in both directions. Truck air brakes take time to engage and the truck needs a long distance to stop, so keep a gap, signal early and avoid sudden moves. Wide, heavy trucks cannot dodge quickly, so never cut one off. If you are leaving the road, wait and exit behind the truck rather than in front of it. After passing, return only when you can see the truck's whole front in your mirror. And expect a truck to swing left before it makes a right turn.

lines.text: Do not linger in turn zones.

narration.text: Do not linger in the area beside a turning truck. When you pass a truck, the pass takes longer and needs more room, and you return only with the truck's full front in view, taking care on hills. When a truck is backing up, wait instead of slipping past through its blind spot. An approaching large truck can fool your sense of its size and speed, so keep to the right. When stopped behind a truck, leave a gap in case it rolls back on a hill, with room to escape. The manual's chart of stopping distances at fifty-five miles per hour rests on brake studies and reaction-time data.

lines.text: Long hoods hide the area ahead.
Return only with the full front in view.

narration.text: Here is the trap. After passing a truck, drivers often move back in as soon as they are past the bumper. The manual warns that long-hood tractors are blind about twenty feet ahead, beyond their deep rear and side shadows, so returns wait for the full front in the mirror and cutoffs stay banned. If you pull in too soon, you are in that front blind zone, invisible to the truck driver and too close for a heavy truck to stop. So keep going until the whole front of the truck shows in your mirror, then signal and move back.

lines.text: All-terrain vehicles and sleds cross at right angles.

narration.text: A reflective orange triangle on the back of a vehicle marks a slow mover, such as an animal-drawn, farm, construction or rural-mail vehicle; pass it with caution. All-terrain vehicles and snowmobiles must stop, yield, and cross roads at a ninety-degree angle. Horses and their riders are protected by rules: riders keep single file to the right, and drivers approach carefully and quietly, never sounding the horn. The chapter's review questions cover truck blind spots, air brakes, passing and backing trucks, children in driveways, blind walkers, cyclists, motorcycles, slow-vehicle triangles and where horses and all-terrain vehicles appear.

lines.text: An orange triangle on a vehicle.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: what does a reflective orange triangle on the back of a vehicle mean? Work it out before reading on. The answer is that it is a slow-moving vehicle, such as an animal-drawn, farm, construction or rural-mail vehicle, so pass it with caution. Remember the other slow road users too: all-terrain vehicles and snowmobiles stop, yield and cross at right angles, and horses get a careful, quiet approach, never the horn. And with large trucks, wait for the full front in your mirror before returning to the lane after a pass.

lines.text: Stay out of truck blind spots.

narration.text: To wrap up, do not linger beside trucks, keep gaps for their long air-brake stops, never cut them off, exit behind them, and expect a left swing before a right turn. Pass trucks with extra time and room, return only when the full front shows in your mirror, wait for backing trucks, keep right when a big truck approaches, and leave a gap behind a stopped truck. A reflective orange triangle marks a slow mover to pass carefully, all-terrain vehicles and snowmobiles cross at right angles, and horses get a quiet, careful approach with no horn. That completes the sharing-the-road chapter.
